faq.q: What is the difference between AC and DC?
faq.a: Direct current flows steadily in one direction, like from a battery. Alternating current keeps reversing, 50 times a second in Britain, and is what comes out of a wall socket.

faq.q: How do the switches in an inverter work?
faq.a: They are power transistors that can turn on and off in millionths of a second. Four switches arranged in an H shape, called an H-bridge, can connect the output either way round, reversing the current.

It means making a wave out of fast on-off pulses of changing length. Where the wave should be high the pulses are long, and where it should be low they are short, so the average follows a smooth curve.
asks: How does an inverter make a sine wave?

faq.q: Why does the grid use alternating current?
faq.a: Alternating current can be stepped up and down easily with transformers, so electricity can travel long distances at high voltage with small losses and arrive at a safe voltage in homes.
asks: Why not use DC for the grid?

faq.a: Modern solar and battery inverters are around 95 to 98 percent efficient. The small amount lost becomes heat, which is why inverters have cooling fins or fans.

facts: Modern solar inverters typically pass on around 95 to 98 percent of the energy they receive.
Mains electricity alternates 50 times a second in Britain and Europe, and 60 times a second in North America.
